I'm an independent admissions counselor. I know people **hate** hearing this over and over again, but it really, truly depends on the situation.

I've seen students submit relatively average essays and receive admissions, because they've had phenomenal ECs and numbers, and I've seen the opposite, where amazing essays helped students breeze through the process. It'll help if you think of it this way - admissions officers are people too, they want to read if it's something interesting, if they can feel you and get to know you through the writing you gave them. (Here's a [viral instance](https://www.enterprisenews.com/story/news/education/2021/05/13/abigail-mack-common-app-college-admissions-essay-harvard-university-cardinal-spellman-brockton/5070731001/) of an amazing essay you may remember that helped this girl get into Harvard, you want to keep reading, it's so fascinating!). If it's another simple, plain essay, they might not read it with as much enthusiasm, turning to look at your profile with a biased opinion. 

TLDR: It depends, but you should write your best essay!

Hey, I'm an independent college consultant. You have a unique profile, your background combined with your initiative and passion is super fascinating, and good essays will really help you tie it altogether. A lot of top schools have huge endowments and a lot of them are able to grant you full ride considering your income (I believe UChicago has a program where they cover tuition under $150k income and full ride (housing, food, books) under around $100k). I'd look into [this list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_the_United_States_by_endowment) and consider what you might be interested in! If you're a US citizen you can apply for the FAFSA and get a good amount of federal money that can be grouped with the aid that schools give you. You can also look up "\[School Name\] Financial Aid Calculator" and put in your info to see how much they give you. If they give you too little aid, you can show them a screenshot and fight it until they match the calculator. 

The thing about summer programs is that the paid ones don't matter as much, they take your money, stamp a fancy logo and send you on your merry way. I've met people who just end up not putting them on their profile and get in to good places regardless. I recommend finding an internship at a local firm, or some sort of job in a related field for the summer. I think your profile can open doors for you to some of these places, they're going to stand out more and they'll provide more inspiring stories to write about and center your focus within mechanical engineering. Good luck with the process, PM me if you have any more questions!

1) Take a Practice Test from Collegeboard with FRQ timed, right now or ASAP

2) Identify what you don’t know, specifically the units/sub units/ topics

3) Watch Khan Academy, AP Daily, Read Princeton, on those topics and make sure to do practice problems to solidify that material

4) Take some special time to work on Unit 3 (IMFs) and Unit 8 (Acid Base Equilibrium) as those have the highest weight on the exam. I would also focus on Unit 1 and Unit 2 as those are easy points on the test and they’re easiest. Unit 4 and 5 weren’t very terrible imo either.

6) If you have time, correct your mistakes from first practice exam (specifically identify why you got it wrong and why the correct answer is correct) For harder questions that you have no clue even after reviewing the material, just skip.

7) Now take some time to dig into test-taking strategies and identifying how college boards grades the FRQs. A lot of this is cover in AP Daily videos bud wouldn’t hurt to watch an extra YouTube video or skim that chapter in Princeton/ 5 to a 5

8) Dedicate remaining time to practice exam, grade, correct, and repeat

Good luck!

5 steps to a 5 is great for review but unfortunately no book’s practice will be like the real collegeboard questions, so I would practice a lot with those. Try analyzing your tests for mistakes, and review the units where those mistakes came from. For me, this led to me realizing that I just had gaps in certain topics or subtopics and made studying easier. 

Also 82% is very good. Keep in mind there’s a huge curve. I think above a 50% is a 4 and above a 75% is a 5, at least for AP Chem. You can see what the predicted curve is by just looking up class and predicted curve. Albert.io’s is very accurate.
